source_text: Ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν ὁ ἅγιος καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πνευματικῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν τὴν πενίαν καὶ τὸν πλοῦτον καὶ τὰ τούτοις ὅμοια ἔταξεν· εἰπὼν γὰρ μακάριοι οἱ δεδιωγμένοι ἕνεκεν δικαιοσύνης σαφῶς ἡμᾶς διδάσκει ἐν πάσῃ περιστάσει τὸν μάρτυρα ζητεῖν· ὃς ἐὰν πτωχὸς ᾖ διὰ δικαιοσύνην, μαρτυρεῖ δικαιοσύνην ἀγαθὸν εἶναι ἣν ἠγάπησεν, κἂν πεινῇ κἂν διψῇ διὰ δικαιοσύνην, μαρτυρεῖ δικαιοσύνην τὸ ἄριστον τυγχάνειν. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ κλαίων καὶ ὁ πενθῶν διὰ δικαιοσύνην μαρτυρεῖ τῷ βελτίστῳ νόμῳ εἶναι καλῷ. ὡς οὖν τοὺς δεδιωγμένους, οὕτω δὲ καὶ τοὺς πεινῶντας καὶ τοὺς διψῶντας διὰ δικαιοσύνην μακαρίους λέγει, ὁ τὸν γνήσιον ἀποδεχόμενος πόθον ὃν οὐδὲ λιμὸς διακόψαι ἴσχυσεν. κἂν τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτὴν πεινῶσι, μακάριοι· μακάριοι δὲ καὶ οἱ πτωχοὶ εἴτε πνεύματι εἴτε περιουσίᾳ διὰ δικαιοσύνην δηλονότι. μή τι οὖν οὐχ ἁπλῶς τοὺς πένητας, ἀλλὰ τοὺς ἐθελήσαντας διὰ δικαιοσύνην πτωχοὺς γενέσθαι, τούτους μακαρίζει, τοὺς καταμεγαλοφρονήσαντας τῶν ἐνταῦθα τιμῶν εἰς περιποίησιν τἀγαθοῦ, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τοὺς καλοὺς τὸ ἦθος καὶ τὸ σῶμα δἰ ἁγνείαν γενομένους τούς τε εὐγενεῖς καὶ ἐνδόξους, τοὺς διὰ δικαιοσύνην εἰς υἱοθεσίαν ἐληλακότας καὶ διὰ τοῦτο εἰληφότας ἐξουσίαν τέκνα θεῦ γενέσθαι καὶ ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων περιπατεῖν κυριεύειν τε καὶ δαιμόνων καὶ τῆς τοῦ ἀντικειμένου στρατιᾶς. καὶ ὅλως ἡ κυριακὴ ἄσκησις ἀπάγει τὴν ψυχὴν τοῦ σώματος εὐχαρίστως, εἴ γε καὶ αὐτὴ αὑτὴν κατὰ μετάθεσιν ἀποσπᾷ. ὁ γὰρ εὑρὼν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ἀπολέσει αὐτὴν καὶ ὁ ἀπολέσας εὑρήσει αὐτήν, ἢν μόνον τὸ ἐπίκηρον ἡμῶν ἐπιβάλωμεν τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀφθαρσίᾳ. θέλημα δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπίγνωσις τοῦ θεοῦ. ἥτις ἐστὶ κοινωνία ἀφθαρσίας. ὁ τοίνυν ἐπιγινώσκων κατὰ τὸν τῆς μετανοίας λόγον ἁμαρτωλὸν τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπολέσει αὐτὴν τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἧς ἀπέσπασται, ἀπολέσας δὲ εὑρήσει κατὰ τὴν ὑπακοὴν τὴν ἀναζήσασαν μὲν τῇ πίστει, ἀποθανοῦσαν δὲ τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ. τοῦτ’ οὖν ἐστι τὸ εὑρεῖν τὴν ψυχήν, τὸ γνῶναι ἑαυτόν. τὴν δὲ μεταστροφὴν τὴν ἐπὶ τὰ θεῖα οἱ μὲν Στωικοὶ ἐκ μεταβολῆς φασι γενέσθαι μεταβαλούσης τῆς ψυχῆς εἰς σοφίαν, Πλάτων δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐπὶ τὰ ἀμείνω περιαγωγὴν λαβούσης καὶ μεταστροφὴν ἐκ νυκτερινῆς τινος ἡμέρας. αὐτίκα εὔλογον ἐξαγωγὴν τῷ σπουδαίῳ συγχωροῦσι καὶ οἱ φιλόσοφοι, εἴ τι τοῦ πράσσειν αὐτὸν οὕτω στερήσειεν αὐτόν, ὡς μηκέτι ἀπολελεῖφθαι αὐτῷ μηδὲ ἐλπίδα τῆς πράξεως· ὁ δὲ ἐκβιασάμενος δικαστὴς ἀρνεῖσθαι τὸν ἠγαπημένον διελέγχειν μοι δοκεῖ τὸν φίλον τῷ θεῷ καὶ τὸν μή. ἐνταῦθα οὐδὲ σύγκρισις ἔτι ἀπολείπεται τί ἄν τις καὶ μᾶλλον ἕλοιτο, ἀπειλὴν ἀνθρωπίνην ἢ τὴν ἀγάπην τοῦ θεοῦ· καί πως ἡ τῶν κακῶν πράξεων ἀποχὴ μείωσίς τε καὶ σβέσις τῶν κακιῶν εὑρίσκεται, καθαιρουμένης τῆς ἐνεργείας αὐτῶν διὰ τῆς ἀπραξίας, καὶ τοῦτ’ ἔστι, πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα καὶ δὸς πτωχοῖς, καὶ δεῦρο ἀκολούθει μοι, τουτέστιν τοῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου λεγομένοις ἕπου.
pass_a_gloss: Our Savior, the Holy One, has ordained poverty and wealth and things similar to these, both for spiritual and for sensory things. For having said, Blessed are those who are persecuted for the sake of righteousness, He clearly teaches us to seek martyrdom in every circumstance. Whoever is poor due to righteousness testifies that the righteousness he loved is good, and even if he hungers or thirsts due to righteousness, he testifies that righteousness is the best thing. Similarly, the one who weeps and mourns due to righteousness testifies that the best law is good. So then, just as He says those who are persecuted are blessed, so also those who hunger and thirst due to righteousness are blessed. The one who accepts the genuine desire that not even hunger can interrupt is blessed. And even if they hunger for righteousness itself, they are blessed; blessed also are the poor, whether in spirit or in wealth, clearly due to righteousness. For He does not simply bless the poor, but those who have chosen to become poor due to righteousness, those who have looked down on the honors here for the sake of acquiring the good. Similarly, He blesses those who have become beautiful in character and body through purity, the noble and renowned, those who have been called to sonship due to righteousness and have received the power to become children of God, and who walk on snakes and scorpions and rule over demons and the army of the adversary. And in general, the Lord's exercise leads the soul away from the body willingly, if indeed it also separates itself from itself through transformation. For the one who finds his soul will lose it, and the one who loses it will find it, if we only put our concern on God's incorruptibility. The will of God is knowledge of God, which is communion with incorruptibility. The one who knows himself according to the word of repentance will lose his sinful soul, which has been separated from sin, and having lost it, he will find it through obedience, seeking it with faith and dying to sin. This then is to find one's soul, to know oneself. The Stoics say that conversion to divine things comes from a change, with the soul changing into wisdom, while Plato says it is a turning of the soul to better things, taking a turn from a kind of night to day. Immediately, it is reasonable to grant an exit to the diligent, even the philosophers, if something prevents him from acting in this way, so that he is no longer left without hope of action. But the judge who has been forced seems to me to deny the beloved and the not beloved. Here no comparison is left, what one would choose rather, human threat or the love of God. And somehow, the avoidance of evil actions and the lessening and extinction of evils are found, as their activity is purified through inactivity, and this is, Sell your possessions and give to the poor, and come follow me, that is, follow the things said by the Lord.

pass_b_english: Our Savior, the Holy One, has ordained poverty and wealth — and everything like them — for both the spiritual realm and the sensory realm. He said, "Blessed are those who are persecuted for the sake of righteousness" (Matthew 5:10), and by that word He clearly teaches us to seek martyrdom in every circumstance. Whoever is poor because of righteousness testifies that the righteousness he loved is good; and even if he hungers or thirsts because of righteousness, he testifies that righteousness is the very best thing. Likewise, the one who weeps and mourns because of righteousness bears witness that the best law is good. So, just as He calls the persecuted blessed, He also calls blessed those who hunger and thirst because of righteousness. Blessed is the one who embraces the genuine longing that not even hunger can interrupt. And if they hunger for righteousness itself, they are blessed; blessed, too, are the poor, whether poor in spirit or poor in substance, clearly for the sake of righteousness. For He does not simply bless the poor, but those who have chosen to become poor because of righteousness — those who have despised the honors of this world in order to acquire the good. In the same way He blesses those who have become beautiful in character and in body through purity, the noble and renowned, who have been called to adoption as sons because of righteousness and have received authority to become children of God, and to tread on serpents and scorpions and to exercise dominion over demons and the army of the adversary. In general, the Lord's discipline leads the soul away from the body willingly, since it even separates itself from itself through transformation. For "the one who finds his soul will lose it, and the one who loses it will find it," provided we place our whole concern upon God's incorruptibility. The will of God is knowledge of God, and that knowledge is communion with incorruptibility. The one who knows himself according to the word of repentance will lose his sinful soul — the soul that has been torn away from sin — and, having lost it, he will find it again through obedience, reviving it by faith and putting sin to death. This, then, is what it means to find one's soul: to know oneself. The Stoics say that conversion to divine things comes from a change, the soul changing into wisdom; Plato says it is a turning of the soul toward better things, a conversion from a kind of night into day. At once the philosophers, too, grant a reasonable exit to the earnest person, if anything should prevent him from acting in this way, so that he is no longer left without hope of action. But the judge who has been forced to act seems to me to deny both the beloved and the unloved. Here no comparison remains — what would anyone choose rather: a human threat, or the love of God? And somehow the avoidance of evil deeds, the diminishing and extinction of vices, is found, as their activity is purified through inactivity; and this is exactly what the Lord says: "Sell your possessions and give to the poor, and come, follow me" (Matthew 19:21) — that is, follow the things spoken by the Lord.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the distinction between spiritual and sensory things, the Stoic and Platonic views on conversion, and the specific theological arguments regarding the soul and sin. Scripture citations (Matthew 5:10 and Matthew 19:21) are correctly added to the English text to identify the quoted/alluded passages.
